!Before class — out-of-date items in the deck (correct these out loud)▾
  • Slide 45 has a math error. The difference in open rates is 0.6 points, and 41,584 × 0.6% = about 250 extra opens, not 1,081. (1,081 is what you get with 2.6%.) The publisher's notes then carry the error forward to "8 or 9 extra leads"; the right figure is about 2. The lesson still holds, and the smaller number makes slide 46's point even better: this test was too small to tell the two subject lines apart.
  • Open rates are unreliable since 2021. Apple Mail Privacy Protection preloads images (including the tracking pixel) for anyone who turns it on, so those emails count as "opened" whether or not a person read them. Apple Mail is a large share of opens, so reported open rates run high. Slide 18 shows marketers moved to click-through rate for this reason. When you teach slides 16 and 43–51, tell students to pick A/B winners by clicks when they can. The math works the same way.
  • Slides 9 and 11 are missing the 2024 sender rules. Since February 2024, Gmail and Yahoo require anyone sending about 5,000+ emails a day to: authenticate with SPF, DKIM and DMARC; offer one-click unsubscribe and honor it within two days; and keep reported spam below 0.3% (aim for under 0.1%). Microsoft added similar rules for Outlook and Hotmail in 2025. These are now the core of "don't get caught in spam filters."
  • Slide 4: the chart runs to 2026 and the publisher's notes say 392.5 billion by 2026; the slide text says 2025.
  • Slide 41: Drift (the exit-survey example) was bought by Salesloft and is being shut down. The email is still a good example.
  • Slide 37: x.ai (the "Amy + Andrew" assistant) shut down in 2021. Again, the email still teaches the point.
  • Slide 47: the formula's second z should be z with subscript 1−β (0.84 for 80% power), and there's a stray, overlapping line of text at the bottom of the slide. Slide 50: the formula is cut off after the last minus sign; slide 51 shows the full version.
  • Slide 52: the publisher's note says the code 2, 4, 8 means "30% off men's sandals." Offer 4 is 50% off. The correct reading is late morning, 50% off, men's sandals.
  • Legal baseline worth one sentence: CAN-SPAM (US) requires a working unsubscribe, a physical address and honest subject lines, and allows 10 business days to honor opt-outs. GDPR (EU) and CASL (Canada) require consent up front. "Never buy lists" is a legal rule in many places, not just good manners.

Slides 1–3Opening

1

Title

Connect it to Chapter 7. Display ads rent attention on someone else's site. Email is the one channel where you own the audience, and no algorithm decides whether you reach them. That's why marketers guard their list so closely.

2

Learning Objectives

Four of them: build a list, write the content, measure the results and stay out of spam filters. Point out that the last one is a prerequisite for the others; a great email in the spam folder earns nothing.

3

Chapter Review (section break)

The plan: why email still matters, spam and how to avoid it, building and cleaning the list, email types and metrics.

Slides 4–6Why Email Still Matters

4

Email Marketing Activity

Check before class

About 347 billion emails a day in 2023, heading toward 392 billion (by 2026; see the correction). The count includes every delivered copy, so one Amazon blast to 10 million people is 10 million emails. Plenty never get opened. Even if only a small share get read, a small share of a huge number is still huge. Ask: how many unread promotional emails are in your inbox right now?

5

Commercial Communication

Survey of U.S. millennials (2022): email is the most-preferred way for brands to contact them, well ahead of text and social media. People will give a company their email address but guard their phone number and their social feeds. Ask students if that's true for them, and whether Gen Z answers differently.

6

High ROI Marketing Activities

Agencies and in-house marketers both rate email as the top channel for ROI. The reason is cost: once you have the list, each extra email is almost free. Email doesn't win because it's exciting; it wins because it's cheap to send to people who already said yes.

Slides 7–9Spam and How to Avoid It

7

Email Spam vs. Email Marketing

Two paths to a list:

  • Black hat: scrape addresses from the web or buy a list, then blast it. Works mainly for products that pull on impulses, because no one rationally buys a lawn mower from a stranger's email.
  • White hat: the customer gives you their address and permission, and you send them things they want: deals, information, entertainment.

The difference isn't the email; it's whether the person asked for it.

8

Catching Spam

Work the 2×2. A filter can make two kinds of mistakes:

  • Spam reaches the inbox (top right): annoying.
  • A real email goes to junk (bottom left): costly. A missed job offer or invoice is worse than one more spam message.

That's why filters lean lax. Ask: if you ran Gmail, which mistake would you rather make? Tie it back: a marketer's job is to look as little like spam as possible, because the filter isn't sure either.

9

Spam Policing

Check before class

Three things watch your email:

  • Mailbox providers (Gmail, Outlook, Yahoo) watch how recipients treat you: do they open, read, reply, or hit "Report spam"? Bad behavior lowers inbox placement for everyone on your list.
  • Spam reporting agencies use spam traps. A pristine trap is an address no person ever used, so mail to it proves a scraped or bought list. A non-pristine trap is an old, abandoned address, so mail to it proves you never clean your list.
  • Filters check content: all caps, exclamation marks, spammy words, a message that's mostly one big image, and sloppy HTML.

Add the 2024 rules from the top: authentication (SPF, DKIM, DMARC), one-click unsubscribe and a complaint rate under 0.3%. Today, getting delivered depends more on who you are and how people react to you than on the words in the email.

Slides 10–13Building and Cleaning the List

10

List Capture 1

Three rules: never buy lists, look for every chance to collect addresses, and get permission. An email address is worth money because every future email to it costs almost nothing. Ask: besides checkout, where could a store collect addresses? (Wi-Fi login, receipts, contests, warranty registration, loyalty programs.)

11

Email List Cleaning

Check before class

Go down the list:

  • Hard bounce (the address doesn't exist): remove right away. Most email platforms do it for you.
  • Soft bounce (a full inbox or a server down): remove after about five in a row.
  • Non-openers: remove people who haven't engaged in a long time, a year at most. Try one "Do you still want these?" email first.
  • Double opt-in (a confirmation click) keeps the list cleaner than single opt-in and protects you from typos and fake sign-ups.
  • Unsubscribe link in every broadcast email; honor it right away (Gmail and Yahoo now require it within two days).

A smaller list of people who open beats a bigger list of people who don't, because the non-openers drag down your sender reputation for everyone.

12

List Capture 2 — Zappos

Two screens. On the left, a pop-up on the mobile homepage. Pop-ups almost always lower conversion, so why would Zappos use one? Because the email address is worth more than the small drop in today's sales. On the right, after a Google sign-in, Zappos asks permission and says what's in it for you (exclusive offers, new arrivals). Ask for permission by selling the benefit, not by saying "Sign up for our newsletter."

13

List Capture 3 — prAna

Same idea, more transactional: 10% off your first order for signing up. That's easy to A/B test (10% vs. free shipping, for example). Point out the gender-interest checkbox. One extra question at sign-up lets you segment the list from day one.

Slides 14–16Email Types and Metrics

14

Email Types

Broadcast emails go to the whole list or a segment; newsletters and promotions are the main kind. Onboarding emails go to new subscribers. Triggered emails go to one person because of something they did. Transactional emails are receipts, shipping notices and password resets. Triggered emails go to one person at a time, but only to people on the list, so they're grouped with the broadcast types.

15

Transactional Emails

They don't need marketing permission because the customer needs them. But the rules are strict: the subject line must say what it is ("Your order has shipped"), the transaction details go first, and any promotion goes after them and takes up less than half the email. Transactional emails get opened more than almost anything else, so a little promotion there is valuable. A lot of promotion turns it into spam.

16

Email Metrics

Key slideCheck before class

Walk each formula:

  • Open rate = opened ÷ delivered. (Inflated by Apple's privacy feature; see the top.)
  • Click-through rate = clicked ÷ delivered, not ÷ opened. Students get this wrong. Clicks ÷ opens is a separate metric, click-to-open rate.
  • Conversion rate = conversions from email ÷ clicks.
  • Average order value = revenue from email ÷ conversions.
  • Churn rate = unsubscribes ÷ addresses on the list.

Quick example: 10,000 delivered, 1,500 opens, 300 clicks, 15 orders, $1,200 revenue. Open rate 15%, CTR 3%, conversion 5%, AOV $80. Revenue per email delivered = $0.12; that's the number that tells you if the program is working. Churn is never zero; every email reminds a few people they don't want it. Don't stop emailing to protect churn.

Slides 17–24Lecture: Writing Emails

17

Lecture (section break)

Transition from the basics to writing emails, building an onboarding sequence and testing.

18

Email Benchmarks

Check before class

In a 2022 survey after Apple's privacy change, marketers named click-through rate as their top success metric. When a metric stops being trustworthy, the industry moves to the next one. This is the reason behind the open-rate correction at the top.

19

Email Parts

Three parts:

  • Subject line: straightforward and descriptive; don't sell in it. Its only job is to get the open.
  • Ad copy: the body. Choose images or text to fit the brand, test the email and check every link before sending.
  • Unsubscribe: easy to find. You can collect a reason on the way out.

Add the preview text (the gray line after the subject in the inbox). Most people see it before they decide to open, and many senders leave it blank. Subject line and preview text together are your ad; the body is the landing page.

20

Online Retail Email — Nordstrom vs. Home Depot

Both lead with one promotion. Nordstrom stops there; Home Depot stacks a dozen more offers below. Which works better? It depends on how many readers care about the main offer. Many Nordstrom shoppers care about a men's sale; very few Home Depot shoppers are buying a garage door this week, so the extra offers ("Ooh, fence installation!") give everyone else something to click.

21

B2B Sales Email

No images, plain text. Ask whether it can still work. (Yes. Plain text looks like a note from a person, and B2B buyers are reading for information.) This is the only full email in the deck, so point out the unsubscribe at the bottom and the request to add the sender to the safe-sender list. Plain text often beats design in B2B because it doesn't look like marketing.

22

Media Email — The Onion

For a media site, an email list is an easy win: the content already exists. The email looks like the website, with several headlines above the fold. The site's traffic data tells the editors which stories to put at the top of the email. Every click is a page view, and page views are ad revenue.

23

Unsubscribe Email 1

A standard form that asks why the person is leaving. Good: it collects data. Missing: an option to get fewer emails instead of none. Offer "less," not just "nothing," and you keep some of the people who were about to leave.

24

Unsubscribe Email 2

Check before class

The opposite problem. Seven checkboxes, and no "unsubscribe from everything." A hard-to-leave list produces spam complaints, and complaints hurt you more than unsubscribes do. Under the 2024 rules, a bulk sender must also offer a one-click unsubscribe, so this design would now cause delivery problems.

Slides 25–27Triggered Emails

25

Triggered Emails

Three triggers:

  • Abandoned cart: remind them of the product; maybe offer a coupon.
  • In-store purchase: a receipt, then complementary products.
  • Past purchase: ask for a review or feedback.

Abandoned cart emails are among the highest-ROI emails there are, because the person almost bought. Sending sooner (within a few hours instead of the next day) usually converts better. Coupon debate: it raises conversion, but customers learn to abandon carts on purpose to get one. Ask: how would you prevent that? (Don't always offer one; offer it only on a second reminder or to first-time buyers.)

26

Triggered Emails cont.

Survey of U.S. marketers (2020) on the tools they use to personalize. Email platforms and A/B testing tie for first (67%); a separate triggered-email tool is used by 38%. Most email platforms now include basic automation, so the gap has narrowed. Personalization based on what someone did beats personalization based on their first name.

27

Effective Email Techniques

Survey of U.S. shoppers (2022) on which retail emails they're most likely to open. Current promotions lead (62%), then shipping and order confirmations (52% each) and delivery confirmations (43%). Three of the top four are transactional: people open emails about something they already did. That's the case for triggered and transactional emails, and for putting a little promotion inside them (slide 15). Review requests (20%) and back-in-stock emails (19%) rank lower than you might expect.

Slides 28–42Onboarding Emails

28

Onboarding Emails

A new subscriber knows less, is more curious and is more responsive than a long-time subscriber. The first few emails set the habit, whether that habit is opening or ignoring. So new sign-ups get their own sequence before joining the regular list.

29

Onboarding Emails Program

Nine possible types; a real program uses 3–5. Decide four things:

  • Which types. Slack needs a friend invite; a clothing store doesn't.
  • Timing. Welcome right away, then spread out (for example 1, 2, 5, 10 days).
  • Dependencies. Someone who clicks everything gets a different path than someone who opens nothing. Never send an exit survey to someone who just upgraded.
  • Content of each email.

Quick exercise: have pairs build a 4-email sequence for a meal-kit service, then for Ancestry.com. The right sequence depends on what the customer has to do next.

30

Welcome

A welcome email with personal touches meant to build trust. Welcome emails have the highest open rates you'll ever get, so say who you are, what's coming and how often.

31

Welcome/Informational

This one welcomes the reader, then makes a small, personal ask that starts a two-way relationship, then links to getting-started information. A small first ask makes the bigger asks later feel normal.

32

Informational/Explanatory 1

Five steps to get started, each with a video or a report. It's a lot for one email, but for a product that takes effort to set up, this is the job. Many programs spread it over several explanatory emails.

33

Informational/Explanatory 2

Video in an informational email. Most inboxes won't play video, so it's really a thumbnail with a play button that links to the video. Video is the easiest way to explain something, and a play button gets clicked.

34

Reengagement/Next Step 1

Sent to people who stalled. This one does four jobs: reminds them, puts the link right in the email, shows their other options and asks them to invite a friend. Most people didn't quit; they got busy. A reminder plus a link is often enough.

35

Reengagement/Next Step 2 — Dropbox

Very short. You didn't install it; here's why you'd want to; here's the download button. One email, one action. There's a link for people who want more detail.

36

Reengagement/Next Step 3 — Hootsuite

More casual and chatty than Dropbox, to fit a "social" brand. It asks for only the next small step, not the whole setup. Compare the two: both work, because each fits its brand and each asks for one thing.

37

Promo Offer

Check before class

A free-trial offer. Offers cost margin, so use them where they change behavior. Many new subscribers would buy without a discount; don't give it to them automatically. This email may have gone only to people whose activity had dropped.

38

Promo Offer/Reengagement — West Elm

"We miss you," 20% off, limited time. It went only to people who ignored earlier emails, so the discount is spent only where a sale was unlikely anyway. Note the handwritten style (it fits a home-decor brand) and the urgency. Target the discount, don't broadcast it.

39

Friend Invite — Nimble

A team CRM is only useful if your team uses it, so a friend invite is essential. This email is longer than the reengagement emails because it asks for a bigger commitment: it includes a case study, then explains how to invite people from inside the app. The bigger the ask, the more convincing the email needs.

40

Upsell — CloudApp

A free-trial upsell. It highlights the free version's biggest limit (a 25 MB file size), right when the user is likely to hit it. Upsell at the moment the free version gets in the way.

41

Exit Survey — Drift

Check before class

Two jobs: learn why they stalled, and make one last attempt to win them back. Short, personal, signed by a person. Even a low response rate is worth it, because the alternative is zero. The ninth type, the social invite, isn't shown because few companies still use it; social follows rarely drive revenue.

42

Email Service Providers

Examples: VerticalResponse, Constant Contact, Mailchimp. Most have free tiers for small lists; you pay as volume grows. You're paying for the mail transfer agent (the sending infrastructure), the database and the sending speed, plus sender reputation and help meeting the 2024 rules. Never send marketing email from a personal Gmail account. You'll hit sending limits and land in spam. Other common names: Klaviyo (e-commerce), HubSpot, Brevo.

Slides 43–51A/B Testing and Sample Size

43

A/B Testing

Check before class

Any decent email platform can A/B test subject lines or content when you build a campaign. This section is based on research by Elea Feit and Ron Berman. The question isn't whether to test; it's how many people to test on.

44

A/B Testing Sample Size

Check before class

The setup: 15% of the list gets A, 15% gets B (about 8,910 each), the winner after 24 hours goes to the other 70% (41,584). Note it picks the winner by open rate; see the correction at the top.

45

Hypothetical Results

Check before class

A gets 12.9%, B gets 12.3%, so A wins by 0.6 points. Sending A to the remaining 41,584 people produces about 250 extra opens (41,584 × 0.006), not the 1,081 on the slide. Have students do the multiplication themselves before you point it out. At a 10% click rate and 8% lead conversion, that's about 2 extra leads.

46

A/B Testing Sample Size cont.

Check before class

Why 30/70? Two forces pull against each other:

  • Bigger test: more people get the losing version (8,910 got B).
  • Smaller test: more chance the result is noise.

Here, the 0.6-point difference isn't statistically significant (chi-square 1.46, p = 0.23). A could have won by luck.

47

Traditional Sample Size Step 1

Check before class

Power = the chance the test finds a real difference when there is one. The convention is 80%. The formula needs the noise in the response (s), the difference you want to detect (δ), significance (α) and power. You have to guess the size of the difference before the test; that guess drives everything.

48

Traditional Sample Size Step 2

Plug in: 95% confidence (1.96), 80% power (0.84), a 15% open rate and a 1-point difference. 2 × (2.8)² × (0.15 × 0.85) ÷ 0.01² ≈ 20,000 per version. Let that sink in: 40,000 people just to test a subject line.

49

Traditional Sample Size Step 3

A free online calculator (AB Tasty) confirms about 20,156. "Minimum detectable effect 6.67%" is the same 1 point, stated as a percentage of 15%. Then ask the real question: most companies have fewer than 40,000 subscribers. Should they never test?

50

Profit-Maximizing A/B Tests

Check before class

Feit and Berman's answer ("Test & Roll," Marketing Science, 2019). Pick the test size that maximizes total results across the whole list, not the one that maximizes certainty. Then send whichever version did better, even if the difference isn't significant. If the two are so close you can't tell them apart, picking the "wrong" one costs almost nothing. The slide's formula is cut off; slide 51 has the full version.

51

Email A/B Test Sample Size

Key slideCheck before class

With a 10,000-person list, the same 15% rate and 1-point difference: about 1,069 per version, then send the winner to the remaining 7,862. The traditional method asked for 20,000 per version, which this list doesn't have. Small lists should test small and act on the result. The same logic works for ad copy and landing pages.

Try it live: how big should the test be?

Use this after slide 51. Change the list size and watch the two methods disagree. Defaults match the deck.

Slides 52–53Exercise: Snappos Email Database

52

Email Database Exercise: Table

Check before class

This goes with the Email Performance Analysis Exercise in the Chapter 8 lesson plan and the database spreadsheet in the Instructor/Student Resources. Make sure students can decode a row before they start. Example: codes 2, 4, 8 mean late morning, 50% off, men's sandals (the publisher's note says 30%; that's wrong).

53

Email Database Exercise: Questions

Five questions. What to look for:

  1. Who to remove: hard bounces, repeated soft bounces, long-term non-openers and anyone who unsubscribed.
  2. Best time of day: compare click and conversion rates by time, not just opens.
  3. Best offer: compare conversion rate and revenue, not just clicks. A BOGO can win clicks and lose margin.
  4. Split by gender? Check the data first. Some people buy for a partner or family. Segment by what people actually clicked and bought, not by an assumption.
  5. The high-heels sale: send it to people who clicked or bought heels or women's dress shoes, plus similar categories, not to the whole women's segment.

Close with the theme: the list is the asset, so treat it like one: earn it, clean it, segment it and test on it.
